title: Scientists Found a Possible Shortcut to Nuclear Fusion. But There's a Catch Hidden in Reactor Walls
excerpt: Heating fusion fuel before increasing its density could make ignition easier.
content:
A tiny amount of metal could be standing between us and practical nuclear fusion. And ironically, it’s the very metal engineers use to protect fusion reactors from extreme heat.

That metal is tungsten. It’s tough, has an extraordinarily high melting point, and is widely considered one of the best materials for lining future fusion reactors. But according to new research, even a trace of tungsten entering the superheated fuel could make fusion significantly harder to achieve.

Just one part in 10,000 could roughly double the pressure needed to reach ignition, the point at which a fusion reaction produces enough heat to sustain itself without external heating.

That’s the bad news. The good news is that researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy’s Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) may have found a smarter way to reach ignition.

Their calculations suggest that instead of increasing the fuel’s density and then heating it, fusion reactors could use substantially less energy by doing the reverse.

The 70-year-old rule of fusion

Nuclear fusion powers the Sun and other stars. It works by forcing lightweight atomic nuclei together, releasing enormous amounts of energy in the process.

On Earth, most leading fusion designs aim to combine two forms of hydrogen, deuterium and tritium, at temperatures exceeding 100 million degrees Celsius. At these temperatures, the fuel becomes plasma, a seething mixture of electrically charged particles.

Keeping that plasma hot and confined is extraordinarily difficult.

×

In a tokamak, a doughnut-shaped fusion machine, powerful magnetic fields prevent the plasma from touching the reactor walls. External heating systems raise its temperature until fusion reactions can begin contributing heat of their own.

The ultimate goal is ignition: a state where the fusion reactions supply enough heat to make continued external heating unnecessary.

Scientists have pursued this goal for decades, guided by a principle developed in the 1950s called the Lawson criterion. Essentially, it describes the combination of temperature, fuel density, and energy confinement needed for fusion to sustain itself.

But there’s a problem with treating that criterion as a simple threshold. It tells researchers what conditions they’re aiming for, without necessarily revealing the most efficient way to achieve them.

And real plasma is considerably messier than the models.

A tiny impurity, a huge problem

PPPL physicists Luis Delgado-Aparicio, Masayuki Ono, and Jonathan Menard developed a mathematical framework that accounts for several complications often considered separately in fusion calculations.

These include helium ash that builds up as fusion fuel is consumed, impurities entering from reactor walls, radiation emitted by electrons moving through magnetic fields, and heat escaping from the plasma.

Each can make ignition more difficult.

Tungsten presents a particularly striking example. The metal is a leading candidate for the inner surfaces of future fusion reactors because it can endure extreme temperatures and intense particle bombardment. However, particles knocked loose from those walls can contaminate the plasma.

Once inside, tungsten can rob the plasma of energy by emitting radiation. Because tungsten has a high atomic number, even very small concentrations can have substantial effects.

The researchers calculated that tungsten contamination of just 0.01% could approximately double the plasma pressure required for ignition.

In a magnetic fusion machine, that’s no small inconvenience. Higher plasma pressure relative to the confining magnetic field can increase the risk of instabilities. Under some conditions, the model suggests that the pressure required for ignition could exceed what the plasma can stably sustain.

“When you leave these effects out, you say the design will work fine,” Ono explained in a PPPL statement. “When you put them in, the picture changes.”

The calculations also suggest that extremely strong magnetic fields, sometimes seen as a route toward more compact fusion reactors, can introduce additional radiation losses that complicate ignition.

What if we heat the plasma first?

The researchers’ most promising finding is linked to ignition.

Imagine trying to cross a mountain range. You could head straight over the highest peak, expending enormous amounts of energy along the way. Or you could find a lower pass that gets you to the other side with considerably less effort.

The new model suggests fusion reactors face a similar choice.

Some proposed operating strategies involve increasing plasma density before raising its temperature. But according to the PPPL team’s calculations, reversing that sequence could offer a less demanding route: heat the plasma first. Then add fuel to increase its density.

The mathematical framework identifies a region called the Cordey saddle, essentially a lower passage through the conditions separating externally heated plasma from self-sustaining fusion.

In the idealized case, this passage occurs at a fusion gain of roughly five, meaning the plasma produces five times as much fusion power as the external heating power supplied. That’s not ignition itself, but it may be a useful intermediate step toward reaching it.

The researchers argue that understanding these pathways could help engineers avoid unnecessarily demanding operating conditions when designing future reactors.

A more realistic road to fusion

The new framework also suggests possible ways around the tungsten problem.

One approach involves coating reactor walls with liquid lithium, which may help prevent tungsten contamination while improving plasma heat retention. Another involves spin-polarized fuel, in which the nuclei are aligned to increase the probability of fusion reactions.

Intriguingly, the researchers also found that some of the energy losses that make ignition harder could help prevent excessive temperature increases, potentially making sustained fusion easier to control.

But none of this means a commercial fusion reactor is suddenly within reach.

The research is theoretical, and the team has not yet demonstrated the heat-first approach experimentally. The researchers plan to investigate it further using computer simulations.

There is also an important distinction between achieving fusion ignition and producing useful electricity.

Scientists at the National Ignition Facility in California achieved ignition in December 2022 using powerful lasers to compress a tiny fuel target. But that experiment was fundamentally different from the sustained magnetic confinement envisioned for tokamak power plants, and it did not produce net electricity for the grid.

Commercial fusion still faces formidable engineering challenges, including managing radioactive materials created by neutron bombardment, securing enough tritium fuel, and developing systems capable of operating reliably for long periods.

The PPPL study doesn’t solve those problems. What it offers is a more realistic way to evaluate how fusion reactors might reach the conditions necessary to operate.

And when building a single experimental reactor can cost billions, knowing which paths are likely to fail before attempting them could be enormously valuable. As Ono put it, “Fusion experiments cost a great deal of money, and you do not want to make mistakes you could have caught beforehand.”

The research was published in the journal Physical Review Letters.
